title: Pressure and Peers: Choose What Happens Next
summary: Three everyday situations about family expectations, peer pressure and a friendship wobble. The teen chooses, sees what might happen, and the psychologist leads the discussion.
clinicianNotes: Scenarios are original. They are conversation starters and not a measure of the teen's mental health. There are no wrong answers to shame: every option has a realistic consequence. Draft content: needs review by a licensed psychologist and a cultural fit check before use with patients.

scenarios.title: Compared with a cousin
scenarios.story: At dinner, a parent mentions that your cousin scored much higher than you in the last exams. Your chest feels tight and you want to leave the table. What do you do?

options.text: Say calmly that it was hard for you, that you want to improve, and ask for help.
options.outcome: Your parent goes quiet, then listens. You agree on a small plan together, and you feel lighter.
options.note: Names the feeling and asks for support. Explore what made this possible and who else could help.

options.text: Stay silent and leave the table early.
options.outcome: The moment passes, but nothing is solved. Your parent still does not know how you feel.
options.note: Withdrawal protects in the moment but leaves feelings unspoken. Explore what makes speaking up feel unsafe.

options.text: Shout that you do not care about studies and storm off.
options.outcome: The argument gets louder. Nobody really hears what you need, and the evening ends badly.
options.note: Anger often covers hurt or shame. Explore what was underneath it and what a calmer first sentence could be.

scenarios.keyMessage: One result does not decide a future. Honest, respectful talk with parents works better than silence or anger.
scenarios.discussion: What is one sentence you could say to a parent when comparisons hurt?

scenarios.title: "Just once" at the gate
scenarios.story: Some older boys offer you a vape and say, "Just once, everyone does it." You do not want to, but you also do not want to look weak. What do you do?

options.text: Say a clear no, walk away with a friend, and tell a trusted adult if they keep pushing.
options.outcome: A few of them tease you, but you leave with your head up and in control of your own choices.
options.note: Firm refusal plus a safe adult. Explore who the trusted adults are and how this feels in a group.

options.text: Make an excuse and take a different road for a few days.
options.outcome: You avoid it for now, but the pressure may come back and you still feel uneasy.
options.note: Avoidance buys time. Explore what a longer-term plan could look like.

options.text: Take it "just this once" so they do not laugh at you.
options.outcome: It rarely stays once. Afterwards you feel worse, and more pushed into things you did not choose.
options.note: Fear of rejection drives this. Explore belonging, and what friendships feel safe to keep.

scenarios.keyMessage: Real friends accept a no. A calm, firm no works, and an adult can help if the pressure continues.
scenarios.discussion: What are some polite but firm ways to say no that sound like you?

scenarios.title: A friend goes quiet
scenarios.story: Your closest friend sits with a new group and does not even look at you. You eat alone and feel left out. What do you do?

options.text: Find a calm moment later and ask them privately if something is wrong.
options.outcome: Your friend admits they thought you were ignoring them. You clear it up and plan to sit together tomorrow.
options.note: Direct and private, without blame. Explore how it felt to take the first step.

options.text: Sit alone and tell yourself you do not need anyone.
options.outcome: The day passes, but you feel more alone and the distance between you grows.
options.note: Self-protection that increases isolation. Explore what loneliness feels like and who else is around.

options.text: Tell other classmates unkind things about them.
options.outcome: Other people take sides and the friendship becomes much harder to repair.
options.note: Hurt turning into retaliation. Explore the hurt underneath and what repair could look like.

scenarios.keyMessage: A calm, private conversation is usually the fastest way to fix a misunderstanding between friends.
scenarios.discussion: How can you start a hard conversation without blaming the other person?
